title: Automate game testing with AI
author: HD_HR
selftext:
Seeing as there is a load of games that are being created with AI but definitly no testing occuring with these games being made (prove me wrong), I feel like it's worth sharing a product I made over the last few years.

[https://obvra.com/](https://obvra.com/)

It's not anywhere near a small project, or vibe coded project. This is years, pre-ai development started. 

The goal is to help game developers (like you) find bugs in your games. If you don't plan to release a commercial game, that's not a problem. If you want to utilize AI to help you replay sections over and over so your hands don't bleed, then you may be interested.

There is a free tier but that focuses mostly on analyzing and building the automation sequence rather than running it.

It is most definitly not cheap but me and even free usage costs me but if you think it may serve a purpose to you now or in the future then you can check it out.

comments.author: AlgaeNo3373
comments.body:
>definitly no testing occuring with these games being made (prove me wrong)

Tbh we're kinda at a point now where before we even get the thing back, frontier agents like Codex/CC have already typically done a pathological amount of tests. 

Playing your own game is playtesting too. Just sayin\~

replies.author: Standard_Text480
replies.body: opus 5.5 does tests for every feature on the first step for me

replies.author: HD_HR
replies.body:
When you say every test for feature, I think I understand that part.

You are referring to it making sure each feature works? Does it also test for the 'expected result'? Like if I click 'New Game' and it doesn't actually load the new game for whatever reason, is there a fail safe included.

Or another example is if you equip a weapon and it doesn't damage enemies because it's glitched due to some unknown issue.

replies.author: Standard_Text480
replies.body: both are correct. the test would be that strike = 50 damage. because strike is not yet built and working, the test fails as expected. then you build the feature and run the test again until it passes

replies.author: HD_HR
replies.body:
>frontier agents like Codex/CC have already typically done a pathological amount of tests.

I can't comment on whether this is true or false. If it is, that's great.

But in terms of 'playing your own game is playtesting too', I agree with you completely. It's just very tedious and it's difficult to catch everything you'd like to. 

It's like, I can play the same thing 50 times and then I add a new feature and I don't play that previous part again, unbeknownst, a new bug was introduced. With automation, it's always re-playing sequences you already taught it and it is aware of changes made with game updates as it tracks everything.

All in all, the traditional way will never go out of style so I hope I'm not trying to make it seem like that.

replies.author: AlgaeNo3373
replies.body:
It's a relatively new-ish development with SOTA models and agents, maybe some local models/harnesses are set up similarly IDK. But yeah, the "pathological" part alludes to it being something pretty aggressive these days as part of agentic work. A built in "make no mistakes" if you will. 

With my larger game if I add a new feature/change the UI etc, the testing includes regression tests etc. So fairly good on its own (completely unprompted) at catching the kinda bugs you describe. F.ex it'll go back and update any tutorial text/UI highlights to reflect changes, then hunt for visual bugs via screenshots/play etc. Stuff I'd have tested myself, and didn't ask it to, so we could prototype faster, but it does it anyways by default now :P Just FYI!

replies.author: HD_HR
replies.body:
That's quite good to hear. I think one thing devs can do probably easier is ask to build in those native tools while the game is being built.

Game testing is not linear so it at the end of the day just depends what sort of testing you want to achieve. Some things will be easier to do than others. There isn't a one shoe fit all solution at the end of the day.

One thing as well is unique playstyles. Since we made the game, we know everything and the best way to play but if you watch others play, you'll be amazed how different decisions one can make even though you assumed it to be easy lol.

replies.author: AlgaeNo3373
replies.body:
Big agree, watching people play your game and struggle to figure stuff out that you've become blind to is a gamedev rite of passage haha :)

One issue with testing via AI is they (typically) play the game via the code/back-end. The ability for Astra et al to play it like a human is kinda interesting, but optimizing for AI useability might not overlap well with optimizing for human useability/aesthetics. Or it might have some really useful overlaps. You might want to look into that stuff too (game playing agents), such as Deepmind's SIMA.
